meta.title: Pitching Controversial Ideas
meta.subtitle: How to get a yes when the room starts with a no
meta.description: 15 moves for pitching ideas nobody believes in yet. From the first practice run to surviving universal skepticism. Every card is a concrete step in the game.
meta.author: AI

cards.title: Practice Your Pitch on People Who Can't Say Yes
cards.hook: Every pitch you give to a real decision-maker without having given it ten times first is a waste of your best shot. The low-stakes rooms build the habit — use them.
cards.truth:
The polished pitch comes from failed ones nobody saw.
• You catch weak spots on small audiences before the big room.
• Different listeners hit the idea from different angles — you learn each one.
• The trap is saving the pitch for people who matter — you arrive unprepared.
cards.remember: Practice pitches that nobody hears make the big one better.
cards.theySee: A friend sitting across a coffee table, listening to someone explain an idea they know nothing about.

signals.t: The listener goes quiet and looks sideways — you lost them somewhere.
They ask the same thing again — your explanation didn't resolve it the first time.
Attention leaves mid-pitch — one section is running too long.
They object to something you didn't mean to make the main point — you're unclear.

steps.title: List three low-stakes people
steps.desc: Write the names of three people who have no power over the decision. Text one today.

steps.title: Pitch out loud and record it
steps.desc: Give the full pitch on a voice memo. Play it back and mark the dead spots.

steps.title: Write the two hardest questions they asked
steps.desc: After each practice pitch, write down the two questions you stumbled on.

cards.script: "I'm working through an idea — give me five minutes and tell me where you got confused."
cards.counter:
A polished pitch on a controversial idea signals heavy preparation — but preparation hides gaps.
• Ask for the one part they're least sure about — watch the confidence drop.
• Notice if they pivot away from specifics when pressed.
• An over-rehearsed answer to a hard question is a flag, not proof.
cards.insight: Practice sharpens the words. It doesn't fix a bad idea. The harder question is whether repeated pitching is revealing a gap in the idea that you keep talking past.

cards.title: Disagree Out Loud Before the Official Pitch
cards.hook: Art Bell told his company chairman he completely disagreed with the task force — out loud, on record. That move gave him standing to pitch Comedy Central months later.
cards.truth:
The person who disagrees on record is the one people call when they want a real opinion.
• Breaking with the group marks you as someone with a view worth hearing.
• The people you need to convince later notice who stands for something.
• The trap is waiting for the pitch room — by then you're a supplicant, not a peer.
cards.principle: Cialdini: Commitment and Consistency — Public Stance
cards.remember: One public disagreement earns more standing than ten quiet nods.
cards.theySee: A person in a group meeting saying they disagree with the consensus and explaining exactly why.

signals.t: After the disagreement, everyone pauses — they didn't expect someone to say it.
A decision-maker shifts attention toward you after the statement.
One person gives a slow nod — they agreed but didn't want to say it first.
The most senior person asks you to say more — they want the full thought.

steps.title: Find the one thing you actually disagree with
steps.desc: Before the meeting, write one thing the group believes that you think is wrong.

steps.title: Say it when asked — no hedging
steps.desc: When anyone asks your view, give the real one. Short, specific, no qualifiers.

steps.title: Follow up with whoever reacted
steps.desc: After the meeting, send one sentence to whoever turned toward you or asked to elaborate.

cards.script: "No. I completely disagree, and here's why."
cards.counter:
Someone using public disagreement to build standing is playing a long game before the pitch.
• Ask for the specific evidence behind the stance, not the rhetorical version.
• Check whether this position is consistent with what they've said before.
• A stance with no data behind it is positioning, not insight.
cards.insight: This works once and strongly. The second time you disagree publicly, you need to be right again — or the standing you built disappears faster than it came.

cards.title: Show the Picture Before You Make the Case
cards.hook: Before you explain why your idea works, make the room see it. Logic closes deals. Pictures open minds.
cards.truth:
People decide with what they can picture, then look for logic to back the feeling.
• A concrete image planted early makes the argument feel like confirmation.
• The room fills in the positive version before you've explained anything.
• The trap is opening with data — the room shuts down before the picture forms.
cards.remember: A picture in their head beats a rational argument every time.
cards.theySee: A presenter describing a specific scene of one person using the finished thing, in plain words, before any data appears.

signals.t: The listener physically moves toward you when you describe the scene.
They start asking about specific users or buyers — they can see it now.
They start adding to the idea before you finish — the picture took hold.
After you describe the scenario, there's a pause before any objection comes.

steps.title: Write a one-paragraph scene
steps.desc: Describe one specific person using your idea in plain words. No abstract terms.

steps.title: Open with that scene — nothing before it
steps.desc: Give the scene before you say anything about market size, cost, or rationale.

steps.title: Watch for the first question
steps.desc: If they ask a 'how' question, the picture landed. If they ask 'why,' go back to the scene.

cards.script: "Picture this: it's late night, you can't sleep, you want to laugh — you turn on one channel and that's all it does, all night."
cards.counter:
A vivid opening scene triggers your decision instinct before your critical thinking turns on.
• Slow down and ask for numbers before you react to the feeling.
• The picture is designed to feel like proof — it isn't.
• Ask: what's the version of this story where it fails?
cards.insight: The picture only needs to hold for ninety seconds — long enough to get past the room's first reflex no. After that, you still need the logic. Making the logic as strong as the picture was is the harder move.

cards.title: Say Their Objection Out Loud Before They Do
cards.hook: Everyone in the room is sitting on 'it can't be done.' If you say it first, you control how it lands.
cards.truth:
Naming their objection first strips it of the energy they'd use against you.
• You control the wording, the timing, and how it gets answered.
• The skeptic can't surprise you with the thing you already said out loud.
• The trap is waiting — by then they own the objection and you're defending.
cards.remember: Name the objection first. You take away their weapon.
cards.theySee: A pitcher saying 'I already know what you're about to say' and naming the exact concern before anyone else does.

signals.t: A skeptic who was physically closed off relaxes after you name their objection.
A brief look of surprise crosses the room — they didn't expect you to say it.
When you name it, two or three people nod — you named the room's real concern.
After you name and answer it, the skeptic doesn't raise a new version of the same point.

steps.title: Write the three worst objections before the pitch
steps.desc: List the three most damaging things the room could say. Write them in the room's words.

steps.title: Open with the worst one
steps.desc: Name the top objection in the first two minutes. Say it before anyone else can.

steps.title: Answer it in one sentence
steps.desc: After naming it, give one direct sentence on why it doesn't kill the idea.

cards.script: "I know the first thing most people say is: there's already too much comedy on TV — so let me show you why that's actually the argument for this, not against it."
cards.counter:
When a pitcher names your objection for you, check if they actually answered it or just made it feel answered.
• Ask the objection again in your own words after they finish.
• Notice if their answer addresses the real version or just the surface one.
• Naming the objection without answering it is a trick, not an argument.
cards.insight: You can name the objection without having a good answer — and the room often doesn't notice until later. The test is whether your answer is as confident as your naming was.

cards.title: Pick One Core Point and Trust It Completely
cards.hook: The pitcher didn't say 'I have five approaches.' She said: my screwball — I don't care if that's controversial, it's my best pitch. A room can smell hedging from across the table.
cards.truth:
Conviction on one clear point is more persuasive than careful balance across five.
• A single committed position is easier to say yes to than a menu of options.
• The listener reads confidence on one point as competence on all of them.
• The trap is spreading across five points — you signal you're not sure which one matters.
cards.remember: One idea you fully believe beats five ideas you're not sure about.
cards.theySee: A pitcher who says one thing with full conviction and doesn't soften it when challenged.

signals.t: When you commit to one point, people stop moving in their chairs.
They ask a detail question about the one point — they're engaged, not dismissing.
Because you didn't spread thin, there's no soft target for them to hit.
The room holds eye contact during the committed point — they believe you believe it.

steps.title: Find your one point
steps.desc: Write the single strongest argument for your idea. Cross out everything that isn't that.

steps.title: Cut every hedge word
steps.desc: Read your pitch draft. Delete every 'might,' 'could,' 'perhaps,' and 'one option is.'

steps.title: Say the one point first and last
steps.desc: Open the pitch with it. Close with it. Everything in the middle supports it.

cards.script: "I'm not pitching five ideas here. There's one move I know works, and I'm going to show you why."
cards.counter:
A pitcher who sounds completely sure of one point may have cleared the field by cutting the evidence that didn't fit.
• Ask what the strongest version of the opposing case is.
• If they can't give it, their confidence is selection, not clarity.
• One committed point makes you want to agree — slow down before you do.
cards.insight: The pitch gets easier when you cut to one point. The harder move is choosing which one — and living with having left the others on the table.

cards.title: Pitch Everyone Before You Pitch the Decision-Maker
cards.hook: Art Bell talked about his comedy channel idea for years before the formal pitch — to coworkers, the finance team, anyone who'd listen. By the time he walked into the room that mattered, the words came without effort.
cards.truth:
Wide early pitching builds your language and shows you where the real resistance lives.
• Different people hit the idea from different angles — you learn all of them.
• Your friend's version of the objection is different from the CFO's — both matter.
• The trap is saving the pitch — you do live testing on your best opportunity.
cards.principle: Cialdini: Social Proof — Breadth of Exposure
cards.remember: Practice the pitch everywhere before the room that decides.
cards.theySee: A person telling their idea to a friend, a skeptical coworker, and an industry expert on three separate days.

signals.t: Two different backgrounds raise the same concern — it's a real problem to fix.
Someone with no industry knowledge immediately sees the point — the idea has broad pull.
Someone close to the industry shuts it down quickly — there's a specific obstacle to address.
You lose your place at the same moment twice — that section needs to be rebuilt.

steps.title: List five people who are NOT the decision-maker
steps.desc: Write names across different backgrounds: a friend, a skeptic, an expert, a non-expert, a stranger.

steps.title: Pitch two of them today with no notes
steps.desc: Say the idea out loud. No slides. Time yourself.

steps.title: Write where you lost them
steps.desc: After each pitch, write one sentence: the exact moment their attention dropped.

cards.script: "I'm testing an idea — it'll take three minutes. Tell me the first thing that seems wrong with it."
cards.counter:
When someone pitches you a polished version of a controversial idea, ask when they first had the idea.
• A long gap between conception and formal pitch means it has been stress-tested — respect that.
• A pitch that feels very new is usually less developed than it sounds.
• Ask who else has heard it and what they said.
cards.insight: Pitching widely doesn't just refine the words — it builds a small group who heard it early and liked it. Those people are now informal advocates before the room even assembles. The next question is whether you know who they are and can reach them.

cards.title: Build the Numbers Case for the Skeptic in the Room
cards.hook: Pictures open the door. The CFO in the room will not walk through it without a rational argument. Know which person needs the numbers and hand them the numbers.
cards.truth:
In any group pitch, at least one person is paid to find holes in the logic.
• That person's silence or objection sets the tone for everyone else in the room.
• A clean rational case gives them permission to agree with what they already feel.
• The trap is assuming one enthusiast covers you with the full room — it never does.
cards.remember: In every room, one person needs the numbers. Have them ready.
cards.theySee: A skeptic at the end of the table who hasn't reacted yet, waiting for one specific thing to change their mind.

signals.t: One person starts writing when you give data — they're building their own internal case.
Someone asks for margin or downside specifics — they want the logic to hold.
The room keeps checking one person who hasn't reacted — they're the real decision.
After you give a number, there's a pause — they're checking it mentally.

steps.title: Identify who has veto power before you walk in
steps.desc: Find out in advance who can kill the idea. That person gets the rational case built for them.

steps.title: Prepare three hard numbers — not ten
steps.desc: Choose the three most damaging questions the skeptic could ask. Have one data point for each.

steps.title: Deliver the data after the picture, not before
steps.desc: Lead with the vivid scene. Then hand the skeptic the numbers. Reverse this and you lose both.

cards.script: "Here's the number that matters: in 1990, basic cable household reach grew 30% in twelve months. That's the window."
cards.counter:
When someone builds a rational case during a pitch, the numbers are the strongest version available — not the full picture.
• Ask for the downside number, not just the upside.
• Ask when the data was collected and how it was selected.
• The cleaner the data looks, the harder you should push on its source.
cards.insight: The rational case isn't for the room — it's for the one person who has to defend the yes to someone above them after the meeting ends. Build it for that second conversation, not the first one.

cards.title: Find a Place Where This Already Worked
cards.hook: 'It can't be done' breaks the moment you find one place where it was done. The case doesn't have to be identical — it has to be close enough to move the argument.
cards.truth:
A single parallel success short-circuits the 'never been tried' objection.
• It shifts the burden — now they have to explain why your case is different.
• Adjacent proof from a different industry still counts if the logic holds.
• The trap is a weak parallel — a bad analogy makes you look desperate, not prepared.
cards.principle: Cialdini: Social Proof — Proof of Concept
cards.remember: Find one case where the same idea already worked.
cards.theySee: A pitcher saying 'this already happened here' and naming a specific case with a specific result attached.

signals.t: The hardest person in the room asks follow-up questions about your example — they're taking it seriously.
A person starts listing why your case is unlike the example — they've accepted the proof exists.
After you name the proof case, the mood in the room changes from doubt to possibility.
Nobody offers a case where the same thing failed — the objection lost its footing.

steps.title: Find three parallel cases before the pitch
steps.desc: Search for industries where the same basic move worked. Write down the three closest ones.

steps.title: Choose the hardest one to dismiss
steps.desc: Pick the case with the most similarities to your situation in time and context. Drop the weak ones.

steps.title: Name it in the first third — not as a late defense
steps.desc: Introduce the proof case early in the pitch. Don't save it for when you're already losing.

cards.script: "ESPN was called impossible for the same reason — nobody thought a single-format cable channel could hold an audience. They were wrong."
cards.counter:
When a pitcher names a parallel success, they chose that case because it fits — not because it's representative.
• Ask how many similar attempts failed.
• A success case with no failures mentioned is not full evidence.
• The question is not whether it worked once — ask what the success rate across all attempts was.
cards.insight: The best parallel case isn't the most famous — it's the most recent and most specific. The closer the match in time and context, the harder it is to dismiss. Finding that case before you walk in is most of the work.

cards.title: Build the Small Version Before You Ask for the Big Resource
cards.hook: They turned down the Comedy Central pitch until the idea had enough momentum to survive. A spec, a demo, a pilot — anything that proves the idea is real — changes the conversation.
cards.truth:
Decision-makers say no to concepts. They say yes to things they can touch.
• A working version shifts the ask from 'trust me' to 'look at this.'
• Building without waiting for permission signals you'll execute regardless.
• The trap is asking for the big resource before you've built anything — there's nothing to evaluate.
cards.remember: A small working version gets the yes that a full pitch alone cannot.
cards.theySee: A person showing a rough working version of something instead of a slide deck filled with projections.

signals.t: A senior person interacts with what you built — they're evaluating, not just deciding.
The room stops asking 'why' and starts asking 'how much' or 'when' — they believe it works.
A person sends the small version to someone else without being asked — it's moving without you.
Instead of 'it won't work,' they start naming specific things to fix — that's a buying signal.

steps.title: Define the smallest real version you could build in one week
steps.desc: Write what you could build, film, or test this week with no budget and no permissions.

steps.title: Build it before the formal ask
steps.desc: Show up to the pitch with the small version already running. Do not arrive with slides only.

steps.title: Make it easy to share without you explaining it
steps.desc: Give the decision-maker something they can forward to one other person and it speaks for itself.

cards.script: "I didn't wait — here's the version I built last week. Take a look before I ask for anything."
cards.counter:
When someone shows you a working demo before asking for resources, that demo was built to impress — not to test.
• Ask how many people have used it and what broke.
• A demo with no failure stories is a sales tool, not proof.
• Ask whether the small-scale economics translate to the full version.
cards.insight: Building the small version first is the right move — but it also locks you into one interpretation of the idea. Knowing when to change what you built versus when to defend it is the harder call.

cards.title: Go to the Biggest Skeptic Before the Group Meeting
cards.hook: Every group has one person who will kill the idea out loud. If that person is still an opponent when you walk into the room, the room follows them, not you.
cards.truth:
The loudest skeptic is the most powerful tool for or against you in that room.
• A converted skeptic vouches harder than an original believer — they carry credibility you don't.
• A private meeting before the group cuts off the public performance of doubt.
• The trap is ignoring the skeptic and counting on majority enthusiasm — one loud no drowns five quiet yeses.
cards.principle: Greene: Law 33 — Discover Each Man's Thumbscrew
cards.remember: Win the hardest no before the room assembles. Everything after is easier.
cards.theySee: A person requesting a private meeting with the most critical voice in the room before the group pitch happens.

signals.t: Others mention this person's name before you've even asked — they know who controls the room.
The skeptic makes their doubts known informally before any meeting — go there first.
In previous meetings, people pause for this person to respond before speaking themselves.
Someone tells you this person killed the last three new ideas — that's your target.

steps.title: Name the person most likely to object loudly
steps.desc: Before the pitch, write one name: the person whose opposition would cost you the room.

steps.title: Request a ten-minute call before the group meeting
steps.desc: Ask to run the idea by them informally — frame it as listening, not pitching.

steps.title: Ask what would change their mind
steps.desc: In the one-on-one, ask directly: what would this need to have to make sense to you?

cards.script: "Before I present to the group, I want your take first — what's the main thing that would make this a bad idea?"
cards.counter:
When someone requests a private meeting before the group pitch, they're working to neutralize you before the room does.
• Give your honest objection — you'll give it in the room anyway.
• Don't soften your position because they came to you privately.
• If they walk in having quieted you, the group loses its best critical voice.
cards.insight: The converted skeptic is your best ally — but only if the conversion was real. A skeptic who privately agreed and then said nothing in the room didn't convert. They just went quiet. That's a different problem.

cards.title: Acknowledge the Controversy Directly, Then Move Past It
cards.hook: If the room already knows your idea is controversial and you don't mention it, you look like you're avoiding the main thing. Name it first. Move past it in the same breath.
cards.truth:
Avoiding the controversy signals you're not ready to defend the idea.
• Naming it directly removes the room's ability to use it as a weapon against you.
• It shows you've already thought through the hard part — that's what standing looks like.
• The trap is pretending the controversy isn't there — the room is thinking about it whether you raise it or not.
cards.remember: Name the controversy in the first sentence. Don't apologize for it.
cards.theySee: A pitcher opening by saying 'I know this idea is going to get pushback — here's why I'm bringing it anyway.'

signals.t: Several people relax when you name it — they were waiting to see if you'd pretend it wasn't there.

signals.l: Someone nods after you name it
signals.t: At least one person nods at the acknowledgment — they appreciate that you said it.
The skeptic shifts their posture after you name the controversy — their guard dropped a little.
For the rest of the pitch, the controversy doesn't come back — you defused it by going first.

steps.title: Write one sentence that names the controversy
steps.desc: Before the pitch, write the plainest version of what makes your idea controversial. One sentence.

steps.title: Put that sentence in your first thirty words
steps.desc: It goes first — before your credentials, before the scene, before anything else.

steps.title: Follow it immediately with why you're pitching it anyway
steps.desc: One sentence after the acknowledgment: this is why I'm standing here anyway.

cards.script: "I know some of you have already made up your mind this won't work. Give me six minutes before you finalize that."
cards.counter:
When a pitcher names the controversy first, they've chosen the version you're thinking about — not necessarily the most damaging version.
• Ask whether there's a more serious version of the objection than the one they named.
• The controversy they named is the one they've prepared for.
• Check whether there's a different controversy they chose not to name.
cards.insight: Naming the controversy up front shows which version of the objection you're ready to answer. If the room has a different version, you've shown your hand before you were ready to.

cards.title: Use the People You Don't Want to Learn What You Need
cards.hook: The people you don't care about losing will give you the feedback you need most. They have no reason to be polite.
cards.truth:
Low-priority targets give honest data because there's no relationship to protect.
• They push back harder on the parts that are actually weak — not the parts you explained poorly.
• You lose nothing when they say no — that's what makes it worth more than a polite pass.
• The trap is only pitching to people who want to support you — they won't tell you what's broken.
cards.remember: Pitch to the wrong people first. They will tell you what's broken.
cards.theySee: A person walking through a full pitch with a company they have no real interest in working with.

signals.t: The feedback is sharper than what supportive contacts gave you — that's the real signal.
They raise a concern you hadn't heard in any of your other practice pitches.
They say no quickly and name the exact reason — that's more useful than a slow polite maybe.
They point out a problem and move on without cushioning it — the honest version of your pitch's weakest point.

steps.title: Name three targets you'd pitch but don't actually want
steps.desc: Write three names — companies, investors, or contacts you have no real desire to work with.

steps.title: Pitch one this week and write every objection they raise
steps.desc: Go in with a real pitch. After, write every specific thing they pushed back on.

steps.title: Compare their objections to what you already prepared for
steps.desc: Highlight anything they named that wasn't on your list. That gap is the real problem to fix.

cards.script: "I'd like to walk you through this idea — I'm mostly here to hear what you'd push back on."
cards.counter:
When someone pitches you and frames it as gathering feedback, they may be testing language, not actually seeking your input.
• Give the real objection anyway — your feedback is real even if their intent is data collection.
• Watch whether they write things down or just nod and redirect.
• If they ignore the specific objection you raised, they were testing their own confidence, not listening.
cards.insight: The honest objections from people you don't care about are more useful than polite passes from people who like you. The harder move is going back to the people who liked you and testing whether they actually believed it.

cards.title: After the No, Ask What Would Have Made It a Yes
cards.hook: The pitch ended with a no. Most people nod and walk out. The one question you ask on the way out is worth more than the hour you just spent pitching.
cards.truth:
The reason behind the no is the data you actually came for.
• Most rejections come down to one missing piece, not the whole idea being wrong.
• The person who just said no is more direct now than they were during the pitch.
• The trap is leaving without asking — you'll pitch the same broken version next time.
cards.remember: A no with a reason beats a yes with none.
cards.theySee: A person who just heard no standing up to leave and asking one quiet question before walking out.

signals.t: You pack up and exit after the no — you've lost the most honest moment in the meeting.

signals.l: You explain why they were wrong
signals.t: Instead of asking, you defend the idea — now they're less likely to give you the real reason.
'Was it the price?' gives them an easy out — calibrated questions get the real answer.

signals.l: You wait more than a day
signals.t: The window for candid post-rejection feedback closes fast — ask before you leave the building.

steps.title: Stay in the room for thirty more seconds after the no
steps.desc: Don't pack up yet. Look calm. The question comes after a beat, not immediately.

steps.title: Ask one specific question
steps.desc: Say: 'What's the one thing that would have changed your answer today?' Write it down in front of them.

steps.title: Write their answer before you leave the building
steps.desc: Don't trust your memory. Get to the hallway and write the exact words they used.

cards.script: "What's the one thing that would have changed your answer today?"
cards.counter:
When someone asks you this question after rejecting them, they're asking you to build their next pitch.
• Give a real answer — it costs you nothing and shows you what they're actually working on.
• If you genuinely don't know the real reason, say so — 'I don't know' is honest and useful data.
• Vague answers like 'the timing isn't right' are not the real reason — push once for something specific.
cards.insight: The answer to 'what would have made it a yes' is rarely the full truth — but it's closer than anything you'd get on the way in. The harder move is deciding whether to fix the thing they named or to find a different room entirely.

cards.title: Hold the Idea When Everyone Around You Says It Won't Work
cards.hook: Art Bell pitched an all-comedy channel when every person he spoke to called it impossible — coworkers, executives, even his own mother. He held the idea anyway. The channel launched.
cards.truth:
Universal skepticism often means nobody has done the work to check if the idea is real.
• 'Everyone says no' means no one has thought hard enough about it yet — including the skeptics.
• Holding the idea forces people around you to give you a better argument than 'it can't be done.'
• The trap is treating social consensus as evidence — it isn't.
cards.principle: Greene: Law 29 — Plan All the Way to the End
cards.remember: Everyone said Comedy Central was impossible. They were all wrong.
cards.theySee: A person still working on the same idea after months of people telling them it won't happen.

signals.t: Every person you pitch uses almost the same words — it's a reflex, not analysis.
Nobody can name a specific reason it fails — they just know it won't work.
When you ask for evidence, the skeptic changes the subject or says 'I just know.'

signals.l: Idea keeps working in your head
signals.t: You keep solving problems with it privately — the logic holds even when the room doesn't.

steps.title: Write the actual evidence against the idea — not the opinions
steps.desc: List every specific fact that would kill the idea. Not what people said — what the data shows.

steps.title: Rate each fact: does it kill the idea or just make it harder?
steps.desc: Separate 'this makes it impossible' from 'this makes it harder.' Most belong in the second group.

steps.title: Continue only if the real evidence is weaker than the consensus
steps.desc: If the facts don't actually kill it and the opposition is opinion-only, keep going.

cards.script: "I've heard every version of 'it can't be done.' Nobody's given me a specific reason yet. I'm still working on it."
cards.counter:
When someone refuses to stop after repeated rejections, their conviction may be clarity — or it may be attachment to a bad idea.
• Ask whether the evidence against it has changed or only the persistence.
• There's a difference between holding the line and ignoring data.
• Ask: what specific thing would make them stop? If they can't answer, that's a flag.
cards.insight: Holding the idea under pressure is a skill. Knowing whether the pressure is coming from real evidence or from people who just don't understand the idea yet — that's the harder skill, and nobody teaches it.

cards.title: Change the Angle of the Pitch, Not Just the Volume
cards.hook: You've pitched it three times to the same people. They've said no three times. Pitching it louder is not a new move.
cards.truth:
A repeated no from the same audience tells you the starting point is wrong, not the idea.
• Changing what you're asking for changes what the room is saying yes or no to.
• A smaller, faster, cheaper ask can get a yes that the full ask never will.
• The trap is treating pitch skill as the variable when the real problem is what you're asking for.
cards.principle: Kahneman: Reference Point — Reframing the Ask
cards.remember: Same room, same no — change what you're asking for, not how loud you ask.
cards.theySee: A person walking back into the same room with the same idea but asking for a different, smaller, more specific thing this time.

signals.t: Each time you pitch it, the room uses almost identical language to say no — the ask is the problem.
They're not hostile — they just don't move. Polite immovability means the reference point is off.

signals.l: No new questions from the audience
signals.t: Nobody asks anything new — they've already processed the pitch and made a decision.
You added more evidence and they still said no — the problem isn't the amount of information.

steps.title: Write the specific thing they said no to each time
steps.desc: List the exact ask from each pitch. Not the idea — the specific resource or commitment you asked for.

steps.title: Find the smallest possible version of the ask
steps.desc: Write the version of the ask that a skeptic might say yes to just to see what happens.

steps.title: Come back with one sentence that names the difference
steps.desc: When you return, say exactly how this ask is different from the last one. One sentence.

cards.script: "I'm not asking for the same thing. This time I'm asking for six weeks and fifty thousand dollars to prove one thing."
cards.counter:
When a pitcher comes back with a smaller ask, the smaller ask is usually the first move toward the original one.
• Ask what happens after the six weeks — where does this lead if it works?
• A smaller ask that succeeds creates pressure to fund the bigger version.
• Say yes to the small version only if you'd say yes to the bigger one in principle.
cards.insight: Changing the ask is the right move — but only if you understand what the room was actually rejecting. Changing the ask when you don't know the real objection is just a smaller version of the same mistake.
